newsitem.title: TURKEY: OECD sees Turkey '97 budget gap well above target.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees Turkey '97 budget gap well above target.

text.p: Turkey's 1997 budget is likely to show a significant deficit despite the shaky government's pledge to attain a zero-gap, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said.

"Excluding privatisation, the budget deficit is projected to be some 7.5 and seven percent of GDP (gross domestic product) in 1997 and 1998 respectively, significantly above the government's targets," the OECD said in its twice-yearly report.
The budget produced a deficit of around nine percent of GDP in 1996.
The Turkish government, under renewed pressure to resign, aims to attain a balanced budget, relying on an expected sell-off revenue of about $4.5 billion this year.
However, the Paris-based organisation said implementation of the privatisation programme would take several years.

It warned the government that present macro-economic imbalances were unsustainable, urging Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Islamist-led coalition to undertakev structural reforms to rescue the troubled economy, struggling with year-on-year inflation of around 78 percent.

"These targets will be difficult to reach in the absence of more vigorous reform of the deficit-ridden state pension system, improvement of the tax administration and restructuring of state economic enterprises," it said.
The government set up a technical committee last month to draw up a three-year structural programme aimed at lowering inflation below 10 percent.

However economy officials and economists say the efforts have come almost to a standstill due to persistent political crisis and the possibility of early elections this year. The committee has not met since May 16.

"It is very clear that this programme can't be implemented now. Technically we are able to prepare a programme but who will implement it? The programme work has not been shelved but it is idle," said a government official who has taken part in the studies.
The initial plan was to conclude studies in the next three months and submit the programme to the government later this year.
Economists fear that the government will boost public spending, increase farm subsidies and delay public sector price hikes on popularity concerns ahead of elections.
"There must be political stability to implement a stabilisation programme," said Izettin Onder, a professor of economic at Istanbul University.
The OECD also cautioned that the policies of the central bank might put an anti-inflationary programme at risk.

"Since September 1995, the Turkish central bank's apparent goal has been to ensure that the Turkish lira depreciates no more rapidly than inflation differentials against Germany and the United States. However, this target leaves no scope for an effective anti-inflationary monetary policy," it said.
The OECD also expects no significant decline in the current account deficit this year. It predicted the deficit to fall slightly to three percent of GDP from 3.1 percent.
It says the economy is expected to grow by 5.2 percent this year after a 7.2 percent growth in 1996, supported by strong private consumption and a surge in investment.
"Output growth remains high, but present macroeconomic imbalances are unsustainable," the OECD said.
It also noted that the financing of the current account deficit and foreign debt servicing had posed no problem although Turkey's credit rating was downgraded by leading agencies.
